blogPosts.title: Understanding Server Components in Next.js
blogPosts.excerpt: A practical walkthrough of where Server Components shine and how to keep interactivity focused.

content.heading: Start With Boundaries
content.body: Server Components work best when you treat them as a boundary for data, composition, and stable markup. Push browser state down into small islands instead of making the whole page interactive.

content.heading: Keep Client State Local
content.body: The payoff is not only smaller bundles. It is also a cleaner mental model where interaction is obvious because it lives near the controls that need it.

content.heading: Design For Change
content.body: The best split is usually boring: server for durable content, client for transitions, forms, filters, and real-time interface feedback.

blogPosts.title: A Writing System for Technical Ideas
blogPosts.excerpt: How to move from scattered engineering notes to essays with shape, rhythm, and useful examples.

content.heading: Capture Before You Polish
content.body: A reliable writing system lowers the cost of starting. Keep raw notes, examples, and questions in separate places before forcing them into an article.

content.heading: Make The Reader Safer
content.body: Strong technical writing reduces uncertainty. It names tradeoffs, shows failure cases, and gives readers landmarks as they move through the idea.

blogPosts.title: Motion Details That Make Interfaces Feel Calm
blogPosts.excerpt: A small set of motion principles for polished product surfaces without making the UI feel busy.

content.heading: Motion Has A Job
content.body: Good motion gives feedback, explains spatial relationships, and makes state changes legible. It should rarely ask to be admired on its own.

content.heading: Prefer Short Distances
content.body: Tiny movements, mild opacity changes, and consistent easing make a product feel responsive without getting theatrical.
